assumptions.subject: workload
assumptions.statement: 3,000 operations/s at peak, counted across ALL flows — synchronous API calls AND the asynchronous events each payment produces. Roughly 900 authorisations/s drive ~1,350 settlement and webhook events/s behind them.

assumptions.subject: acquirer
assumptions.statement: The card network / acquirer is NOT drawn as its own component: Keystone has no honest per-instance price for a third-party API, so instead the external round-trip is modelled INSIDE the authorisation service — 250 ms of blocking wait and only ~250 auths/s per instance (about 60 concurrent connections). The real dependency also enforces a HARD rate limit that returns errors rather than slowing down, which a queueing model cannot show.

assumptions.subject: ledger
assumptions.statement: ONE PostgreSQL primary is deliberate, not a sizing miss: a double-entry ledger needs a single writer for correctness. It is a single point of failure and the scaling wall of this design — sharding a ledger costs you cross-shard atomicity.

assumptions.subject: cache
assumptions.statement: Redis holds idempotency keys and velocity counters. It is sized for MEMORY and durability, not throughput, which is why its utilisation looks low — do not scale it down on that basis.

assumptions.subject: webhook
assumptions.statement: Merchant webhooks block on the merchant's own endpoint (~200 ms, ~40 concurrent per instance). A slow merchant is a real back-pressure source; retries and dead-lettering are required and not modelled here.

assumptions.subject: headroom
assumptions.statement: Every tier on the money path is held near 50-60% utilisation, not at the 85% ceiling. With a 250 ms acquirer round-trip, running the authorisation tier hot multiplies the customer's wait: at 85% the same call would add roughly 1.4 s of queueing on top of it. Paying for that headroom is the explicit design decision here, and it is why this design costs more than its throughput suggests.

assumptions.subject: compliance
assumptions.statement: Money movement: PCI-DSS scope, chargebacks, fraud rules, reconciliation and exactly-once idempotency are REQUIRED and out of scope for this model. Expert review is mandatory before any production use.

_library.summary: Card authorisation, an ACID ledger, and asynchronous settlement plus merchant webhooks.
